claim: The study reconstructed 78 neurosecretory neurons in the brain of larval Platynereis dumerilii using transmission electron microscopy and gene expression mapping.
source: We reconstructed 78 neurosecretory neurons and mapped their synaptic connectivity in the brain of larval Platynereis dumerilii, a marine annelid.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of neurons reconstructed and the methods used.

claim: The neurosecretory neurons form an anterior neurosecretory center expressing many neuropeptides, including hypothalamic peptide orthologs and their receptors.
source: These neurons form an anterior neurosecretory center expressing many neuropeptides, including hypothalamic peptide orthologs and their receptors.
evidence: The abstract directly states the expression of neuropeptides including hypothalamic orthologs.

claim: Analysis of peptide-receptor pairs in spatially mapped single-cell transcriptome data revealed sparsely connected networks linking specific neuronal subsets.
source: Analysis of peptide-receptor pairs in spatially mapped single-cell transcriptome data revealed sparsely connected networks linking specific neuronal subsets.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the analysis and its findings.

claim: A neuropeptide can couple neurosecretory and synaptic brain signaling.
source: We experimentally analyzed one peptide-receptor pair and found that a neuropeptide can couple neurosecretory and synaptic brain signaling.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from experimental analysis.

claim: Synapse-level connectomics using electron microscopy allows mapping synaptic networks, but fails to reveal non-synaptic signaling.
source: Synapse-level connectomics using electron microscopy allows mapping synaptic networks, but fails to reveal non-synaptic signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the introduction.

claim: Neurosecretory centers such as the vertebrate hypothalamus and pituitary show exceptionally high levels of neuropeptide expression.
source: Neurosecretory centers, such as the vertebrate hypothalamus and pituitary, are found in the anterior brain of many animals and show exceptionally high levels of neuropeptide expression (Herget and Ryu, 2015; Siegmund and Korge, 2001; Campbell et al., 2017) suggesting extensive non-synaptic signaling.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neurosecretory centers coordinate many processes in physiology, behavior, and development, including growth, feeding, and reproduction.
source: These centers coordinate many processes in physiology, behavior, and development, including growth, feeding, and reproduction (Sakurai et al., 1998; Bluet-Pajot et al., 2001; Sternson et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The apical organ in annelid and other marine larvae is involved in the detection of various environmental cues.
source: Annelid and other marine larvae have an anterior sensory center, the apical organ, involved in the detection of various environmental cues (Hadfield et al., 2000; Conzelmann et al., 2013a; Page, 2002; Chia and Koss, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The apical organ is neurosecretory and expresses diverse neuropeptides that are thought to regulate various aspects of larval behavior and physiology.
source: The apical organ is neurosecretory and expresses diverse neuropeptides that are thought to regulate various aspects of larval behavior and physiology, including the induction of larval settlement and metamorphosis (Mayorova et al., 2016; Thorndyke et al., 1992; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Conzelmann et al., 2011; Marlow et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Apical organs have a conserved molecular fingerprint across marine larvae, suggesting that they represent a conserved sensory-neuroendocrine structure.
source: Apical organs have a conserved molecular fingerprint across marine larvae, suggesting that they represent a conserved sensory-neuroendocrine structure (Marlow et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and includes an inference about evolutionary conservation.

claim: The apical organ area in Platynereis larvae shows a distinct molecular fingerprint with similarities to other neuroendocrine centers, including the anterior medial neurosecretory center of arthropods and the vertebrate hypothalamus.
source: The apical organ area or apical nervous system (ANS) in Platynereis larvae shows a distinct molecular fingerprint with similarities to other neuroendocrine centers, including the anterior medial neurosecretory center of arthropods and the vertebrate hypothalamus, suggesting a common ancestry (Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Steinmetz et al., 2010; Conzelmann et al., 2013b; Hunnekuhl and Akam, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and includes an inference about common ancestry.

claim: The study used a full-body serial-section transmission electron microscopy dataset of a 3-day-old larva.
source: We used a previously reported full-body serial-section transmission electron microscopy (ssTEM) dataset of a 3-day-old larva (Randel et al., 2015) and reconstructed its entire anterior neurosecretory nervous system (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: The methods section explicitly describes the dataset used.

claim: The neurosecretory plexus forms an anatomically and ultrastructurally distinct area that can be clearly distinguished from other neuropils.
source: The neurosecretory plexus forms an anatomically and ultrastructurally distinct area that can be clearly distinguished from other neuropils, including the adjacent optic and nuchal organ neuropils (Randel et al., 2014; Shahidi et al., 2015)(Figure 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Neurites in the neurosecretory plexus have a high number of dense-core vesicles and very few synapses.
source: Neurites in this area have a high number of dense-core vesicles and very few synapses (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by reference to figures showing TEM images.

claim: The study identified 70 sensory neurons and eight projection interneurons that project to the neurosecretory plexus.
source: We reconstructed all neurons that project to this region (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1) and identified 70 sensory neurons and eight projection interneurons, the latter project in and out of the neurosecretory plexus.
evidence: The results explicitly state the number of neurons identified and their types.

claim: Most of the sensory neurons are bilaterally symmetric pairs with distinct axonal projection patterns, except for a few asymmetric neurons.
source: Most of the sensory neurons are bilaterally symmetric pairs with distinct axonal projection patterns, except for a few asymmetric neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by reference to a figure.

claim: At least 20 different sensory cell types with likely different sensory functions were distinguished based on morphological criteria.
source: Based on these morphological criteria we could distinguish at least 20 different sensory cell types with likely different sensory functions.
evidence: This is stated as a result of morphological analysis.

claim: There are four ciliary photoreceptor cells (cPRC) with highly extended ciliary membranes.
source: For example, there are four ciliary photoreceptor cells (cPRC)(Arendt et al., 2004) with highly extended ciliary membranes
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation for the cell type identification.

claim: Most of the sensory neurons have axonal projections that are extensively branched within the neurosecretory plexus and are filled with dense-core vesicles.
source: Most of the sensory neurons have axonal projections that are extensively branched within the neurosecretory plexus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and that are filled with dense-core vesicles (Figure 1F).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The pairs of left-right symmetric sensory neurons project to similar areas of the neurosecretory plexus revealing a fine-scale organization within the plexus.
source: The pairs of left-right symmetric sensory neurons project to similar areas of the neurosecretory plexus revealing a fine-scale organization within the plexus (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The study used whole-mount in situ hybridization for 53 and 58 Platynereis proneuropeptides in 2-day-old and 3-day-old larvae respectively.
source: To comprehensively analyze neuropeptide expression in the whole 2-day-old and 3-day-old larvae, we used whole-mount in situ hybridization for 53 and 58 Platynereis proneuropeptides respectively (of 98 total [Conzelmann et al., 2013b]).
evidence: The methods explicitly describe the number of proneuropeptides analyzed.

claim: The region with the highest proneuropeptide expression corresponds to the ANS.
source: We summed all binarized average expression domains and found that the region with the highest proneuropeptide expression corresponds to the ANS (Figure 1H).
evidence: This finding is stated and supported by reference to Figure 1H.

claim: Some voxels in the gene expression atlases co-express up to 10 different proneuropeptides in both 2-day-old and 3-day-old larvae.
source: Some voxels in the gene expression atlases co-express up to 10 different proneuropeptides in both 2-day-old and 3-day-old larvae.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the gene expression atlas analysis.

claim: Proneuropeptides expressed in the ANS region include two Platynereis insulin-like peptides (IRP2, IRP3), two bursicons (bursicon-A, -B), achatin, MIP, and several homologs of hypothalamic peptides.
source: Proneuropeptides that were expressed in the ANS region include two Platynereis insulin-like peptides (IRP2, IRP3), two bursicons (bursicon-A, -B), achatin, MIP, and several homologs of hypothalamic peptides (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Jékely, 2013) including NPY (three homologs, NPY1, NPY4, NKY2), orexin/allatotropin, tachykinin, galanin/allatostatin-A, and allatostatin-C/somatostatin (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations for the homology assignments.

claim: The majority of proneuropeptides (34 genes) had very similar expression patterns between 2-day-old trochophore and 3-day-old nectochaete larval stages.
source: The majority of proneuropeptides (34 genes) had very similar expression patterns between 2-day-old trochophore and 3-day-old nectochaete larval stages (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparing expression patterns across stages.

claim: A number of proneuropeptides (17 genes) showed a prominent expansion in spatial expression domain between 2-day-old and 3-day-old stages.
source: Apart from this trend, a number of proneuropeptides (17 genes) showed a prominent expansion in spatial expression domain between 2-day-old and 3-day-old stages.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparing expression patterns across stages.

claim: Expansions of gene expression were mainly in the dorsolateral area of the larval head, possibly reflecting the differentiation of further peptidergic neurons in this region during development.
source: Expansions of gene expression were mainly in the dorsolateral area of the larval head, possibly reflecting the differentiation of further peptidergic neurons in this region during development.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Neuropeptide expression was mapped to 26 reconstructed ANS neurons.
source: Overall, we mapped neuropeptide expression to 26 reconstructed ANS neurons, including sensory neurons co-expressing IRP2 and FMRFamide (SNIRP2-FMRF), IRP2 and bursicon (SNIRP2-burs), or expressing ASTC/somatostatin (SNASTC1) (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result of correlating gene expression with reconstructed neurons.

claim: 33% of the ANS neurons have 0–2 synapses despite highly branched axonal projections filled with dense core vesicles.
source: 33% of the neurons have 0–2 synapses despite highly branched axonal projections filled with dense core vesicles (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the synaptic connectivity analysis.

claim: Most ANS neurons predominantly use volume transmission.
source: This suggests that these neurons predominantly use volume transmission.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the low number of synapses.

claim: The synapses identified in most neurons contained dense-core vesicles, indicative of their peptidergic nature.
source: The synapses we identified in most neurons contained dense-core vesicles, indicative of their peptidergic nature.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with an interpretation based on vesicle type.

claim: The four cPRCs, an asymmetric sensory neuron (SN47Ach), and the eight projection neurons have the highest number of synapses.
source: The four cPRCs, an asymmetric sensory neuron (SN47Ach), and the eight projection neurons have the highest number of synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the synaptic connectivity analysis.

claim: 15 ANS sensory neurons have 10 or more peptidergic synapses.
source: In addition, 15 ANS sensory neurons have 10 or more peptidergic synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the synaptic connectivity analysis.

claim: The cPRCs express a cholinergic marker and contain large synapses with clear vesicles as well as dense core vesicles.
source: The cPRCs express a cholinergic marker (Jékely et al., 2008) and contain large synapses with clear vesicles as well as dense core vesicles.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation for the cholinergic marker.

claim: The eight projection neurons contain large synapses with clear vesicles and dense core vesicles.
source: The eight projection neurons also contain large synapses with clear vesicles and dense core vesicles.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: The study used an experimentally determined list of 18 deorphanized Platynereis neuropeptide GPCRs.
source: The GPCR list included 18 deorphanized neuropeptide receptors.
evidence: This is stated as part of the methods for analyzing peptidergic signaling networks.

claim: The study deorphanized three additional neuropeptide receptors: a corazonin receptor, and second receptors for vasotocin and myomodulin.
source: To this we added a further three deorphanized neuropeptide receptors. We deorphanized a corazonin receptor activated by both Platynereis corazonin-1 (CRZ1) and corazonin-2 (CRZ2), originally described as GnRH1 and GnRH2 (Conzelmann et al., 2013a) but renamed to follow the nomenclature in (Zandawala et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2016; Hussain et al., 2016), and second receptors for vasotocin and myomodulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result of receptor deorphanization experiments.

claim: The combined expression of 80 proneuropeptides showed a highly peptidergic group of cells in the ANS region.
source: The combined expression of 80 proneuropeptides showed a similar pattern to the in situ hybridisation map with a highly peptidergic group of cells in the ANS region, as defined by the endocrine marker genes Phc2, dimmed, Otp and nk2.1 (Conzelmann et al., 2013a; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the single-cell transcriptome analysis.

claim: Most GPCR expression was concentrated in the ANS in peptidergic cells.
source: Most GPCR expression was also concentrated in the ANS in peptidergic cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the single-cell transcriptome analysis.

claim: Several cells expressed a unique combination of up to nine deorphanized GPCRs.
source: Several cells expressed a unique combination of up to nine deorphanized GPCRs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the single-cell transcriptome analysis.

claim: The chemical connectivity maps of individual ligand-receptor pairs show very sparse and specific chemical wiring.
source: The chemical connectivity maps of individual ligand-receptor pairs show very sparse and specific chemical wiring.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the peptidergic network analysis.

claim: On average, less than 1% of all potential connections are realized (0.8% graph density averaged for all peptide-receptor pairs).
source: On average, less than 1% of all potential connections are realized (0.8% graph density averaged for all peptide-receptor pairs).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the network analysis.

claim: Single cells expressing many different neuropeptides generally link to non-overlapping target nodes by each peptide-receptor channel.
source: Single cells expressing many different neuropeptides generally link to non-overlapping target nodes by each peptide-receptor channel (Figure 3O and Figure 3—figure supplement 4Q).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the peptidergic network analysis.

claim: Multiple signals can converge on one cell that expresses more than one GPCR.
source: Conversely, multiple signals can converge on one cell that expresses more than one GPCR (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the peptidergic network analysis.

claim: The combined multichannel peptidergic connectome of 23 receptor-ligand pairs forms a single network with an average clustering coefficient of 0.49 and an average minimum path length of 1.54, forming a small-world network.
source: The combined multichannel peptidergic connectome of 23 receptor-ligand pairs forms a single network with an average clustering coefficient of 0.49 and an average minimum path length of 1.54, forming a small-world network (Watts and Strogatz, 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the network analysis with a citation for the small-world network concept.

claim: The three neuron types with the highest weighted in-degree and authority value include a pair of dorsal sensory neurons, a central pair of IRP2 neurons, and a pair of RGWamide-expressing neurons.
source: The three neuron types with the highest weighted in-degree and authority value include a pair of dorsal sensory neurons, a central pair of IRP2 neurons, and a pair of RGWamide-expressing neurons (Figure 3M and Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the network analysis.

claim: The IRP2 neurons are under the influence of an NPY peptide and EFLGamide, the Platynereis homolog of thyrotropin-releasing hormone, and express 20 different proneuropeptides.
source: The IRP2 neurons are under the influence of an NPY peptide and EFLGamide, the Platynereis homolog of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (Bauknecht and Jékely, 2015) and express 20 different proneuropeptides.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a citation for the homology assignment.

claim: Co-expression analysis revealed 1 cell (1% of total) with only neurotransmitter markers but no neuropeptide, 76 (71% of total) purely peptidergic cells, and 21 cells that co-express small transmitters and neuropeptides (19.6% of total).
source: Co-expression analysis with small neurotransmitter synthesis enzymes revealed 1 cell (1% of total) with only neurotransmitter markers but no neuropeptide, 76 (71% of total) purely peptidergic cells, and 21 cells that co-express small transmitters and neuropeptides (19.6% of total)(Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the co-expression analysis.

claim: 2 ANS cells co-express up to 24 different proneuropeptides.
source: Strikingly, 2 ANS cells co-express up to 24 different proneuropeptides.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the single-cell transcriptome analysis.

claim: 15 cells from the spatially mapped single cell transcriptome dataset were correlated to ANS cells reconstructed from ssTEM data.
source: Based on specific neuropeptide expression and the spatial mapping we could correlate 15 cells from the spatially mapped single cell transcriptome dataset to ANS cells reconstructed from our ssTEM data (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result of correlating the two datasets.

claim: Comparison of Platynereis ANS and mouse hypothalamus single-cell transcriptomes identified significant coexpression for a subset of genes marking a cell population with a likely function in regulating circadian oscillations.
source: By comparing the expression across cells of orthologous neuropeptides, neuropeptide receptors, transcription factors and other marker genes in these data sets (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), we identified significant coexpression for a subset of genes in both mouse and Platynereis marking a cell population with a likely function in regulating circadian oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis with an inference about function.

claim: In all three datasets the genes bmal/arntl, otp, synaptotagmin/syt5, and 7B2/SCG5 showed significant co-expression.
source: In all three datasets the genes bmal/arntl, otp, synaptotagmin/syt5, and 7B2/SCG5 showed significant co-expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: In both the Romanov et al. mouse data and the Platynereis data, these genes are also co-expressed with ASTA2/galanin neuropeptide.
source: In both the Romanov et al. mouse data and the Platynereis data, these genes are also co-expressed with ASTA2/galanin neuropeptide.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: The bmal gene encodes an important component of the circadian clock in flies and vertebrates.
source: The bmal gene encodes an important component of the circadian clock in flies and vertebrates (Van Gelder et al., 2003) and is expressed in the Platynereis ANS, in the same region as several other circadian clock markers (Arendt et al., 2004; Tosches et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: Co-expression correlation analyses revealed co-expression in all three datasets of the neuropeptide pair ASTC/somatostatin and sulfakinin/cholecystokinin.
source: Co-expression correlation analyses of the two datasets also revealed co-expression in all three datasets of the neuropeptide pair ASTC/somatostatin and sulfakinin/cholecystokinin.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: Neuropeptide pairs ASTA2/galanin and glycoprotein beta/Gpha2, and NPY and ASTC/somatostatin showed co-expression in both the Romanov et al. mouse and the Platynereis datasets.
source: Additionally, neuropeptide pairs ASTA2/galanin and glycoprotein beta/Gpha2, and NPY and ASTC/somatostatin showed co-expression in both the Romanov et al. mouse and the Platynereis datasets.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: The RGWamide-expressing neurons express VAChT, two NPY receptors (NPY4 and NKY), an achatin receptor, and 17 proneuropeptide genes.
source: Based on the spatially mapped Platynereis single cell transcriptome dataset, the RGWamide-expressing neurons express VAChT, two NPY receptors (NPY4 and NKY), an achatin receptor, and 17 proneuropeptide genes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the single-cell transcriptome analysis.

claim: The RGWamide-expressing cells were identified as INRGW projection neurons by position and RGWamide-expression.
source: By position and RGWamide-expression we identified these cells in our TEM reconstruction as INRGW projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a result of correlating gene expression with reconstructed neurons.

claim: The four INRGW projection interneurons and the four INNOS projection interneurons lack sensory dendrites or cilia.
source: The four INRGW projection interneurons as well as the four INNOS projection interneurons have a distinct anatomy (Figure 4B). They lack sensory dendrites or cilia
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: The axons of INRGW and INNOS projection interneurons are extensively branched, spreading around the circumference of the ANS neuropil and projecting posteriorly out of this area to the ventral neuropil of the synaptic nervous system.
source: and their axons are extensively branched, spreading around the circumference of the ANS neuropil and projecting posteriorly out of this area to the ventral neuropil of the synaptic nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: The INRGW cells form many large (likely cholinergic) synapses with clear synaptic vesicles on two serotonergic ciliomotor neurons (Ser-h1).
source: Here the INRGW cells form many large (likely cholinergic) synapses with clear synaptic vesicles on two serotonergic ciliomotor neurons (Ser-h1)(Figure 4C) that are known to play a role in the regulation of ciliary beating (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction with a citation for the function of Ser-h1 neurons.

claim: The axons of the INRGW cells are filled with dense core vesicles throughout the region where they innervate the neuropil.
source: The axons of the INRGW cells are also filled with dense core vesicles throughout the region where they innervate the neuropil (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: No peptidergic synapses were evident in the INRGW cells.
source: These vesicles accumulate in bulbous thickenings of the INRGW neurites, however no peptidergic synapses were evident in these cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: The INRGW cells can signal either synaptically with neurotransmitters or via peptidergic endocrine release.
source: This indicates that the INRGW cells can signal either synaptically with neurotransmitters or via peptidergic endocrine release.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the presence of both clear and dense core vesicles.

claim: The INNOS cells only synapse on the INRGW cells in the ventral neuropil.
source: The INNOS cells only synapse on the INRGW cells in the ventral neuropil.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: The INNOS cells synapse on the INRGW cells with mixed clear and dense core vesicle synapses.
source: The INNOS cells synapse on the INRGW cells with mixed clear and dense core vesicle synapses (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: The INRGW neurons receive synapses in the ventral neuropil area from two non-ANS neurons (cMNvl and pygPBbicil) that belong to the ciliomotor circuit of the larva.
source: The INRGW neurons also receive synapses in the ventral neuropil area from two non-ANS neurons. These neurons (cMNvl and pygPBbicil) belong to the ciliomotor circuit of the larva (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: From the ANS, the INRGW projection neurons receive small transmitter synapses from the cPRC cells, mixed clear and dense core vesicle synapses from the SN47Ach neuron in the ventral neuropil, and peptidergic synapses from three other ANS sensory neurons in the neurosecretory plexus.
source: From the ANS, the INRGW projection neurons receive small transmitter synapses from the cPRC cells, mixed clear and dense core vesicle synapses from the SN47Ach neuron in the ventral neuropil, and peptidergic synapses from three other ANS sensory neurons in the neurosecretory plexus (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the reconstruction.

claim: The INRGW and INNOS neurons express seven deorphanized GPCRs, including a receptor for achatin that is specifically activated by achatin peptide containing a D-amino acid.
source: The INRGW and INNOS neurons express seven deorphanized GPCRs (Figure 4F), including a receptor for achatin that is specifically activated by achatin peptide containing a D-amino acid (Bauknecht and Jékely, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a citation for the receptor specificity.

claim: When larvae were treated with D-achatin, neurons in the ANS were rhythmically activated.
source: When we treated larvae with D-achatin, neurons in the ANS were rhythmically activated.
evidence: This is stated as a result from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The rhythmically activated neurons correspond by position to the INRGW cells.
source: These neurons correspond by position to the INRGW cells (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the position of activated neurons.

claim: The rhythmic activation was in-phase with the activation of the Ser-h1 neurons and a ventral motorneuron (vMNasync), but out of phase with the main cholinergic motorneuron of the head ciliary band, the MC neuron.
source: The rhythmic activation was in-phase with the activation of the Ser-h1 neurons and a ventral motorneuron (vMNasync), but out of phase with the main cholinergic motorneuron of the head ciliary band, the MC neuron (readily identifiable by calcium imaging [Verasztó et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is stated as a result from calcium imaging experiments with a citation for MC neuron identification.

claim: A similar effect was not observed upon L-achatin treatment.
source: We could not observe a similar effect upon L-achatin treatment (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Platynereis larvae have a cholinergic and a serotonergic ciliomotor circuit that oscillate out-of-phase.
source: Platynereis larvae have a cholinergic and a serotonergic ciliomotor circuit that oscillate out-of-phase.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The cholinergic phase arrests the cilia and the serotonergic phase correlates with ciliary beating.
source: The cholinergic phase arrests the cilia and the serotonergic phase correlates with ciliary beating (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior research.

claim: Correlation analysis revealed that D-achatin coupled the activity of the INRGW cells to the serotonergic cells, and increased the negative correlation between the activity patterns of serotonergic neurons and the MC neuron.
source: Correlation analysis of neuronal activity patterns revealed that D-achatin coupled the activity of the INRGW cells to the serotonergic cells, and increased the negative correlation between the activity patterns of serotonergic neurons and the MC neuron (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from correlation analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: The Platynereis larval ANS has a low degree of synaptic connectivity, a strong neurosecretory character, and a high diversity of neuropeptide expression.
source: We found that the Platynereis larval ANS has a low degree of synaptic connectivity, a strong neurosecretory character, and a high diversity of neuropeptide expression.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: The ANS is wired primarily chemically and not synaptically.
source: This suggests that the ANS is wired primarily chemically and not synaptically.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the low synaptic connectivity.

claim: Very specific peptidergic links were identified that connect only a small subset of ANS neurons.
source: We identified very specific peptidergic links based on proneuropeptide and GPCR transcript expression that connect only a small subset of ANS neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the peptidergic network analysis.

claim: Most peptidergic signaling in the brain occurs within the ANS.
source: Strikingly, it is not only the proneuropeptides that are expressed with high diversity in the ANS, but also their receptors, suggesting that most peptidergic signaling in the brain occurs within the ANS.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the high diversity of both peptides and receptors in the ANS.

claim: The ANS undergoes autoregulation at the level of single cells or cellular subpopulations.
source: Through our analysis of peptidergic signaling networks in the ANS, we could also find evidence that the ANS undergoes autoregulation, at the level of single cells or cellular subpopulations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the peptidergic network analysis.

claim: Autoregulation of cells in the ANS can occur through allatotropin/orexin, NPY4, achatin, diuretic hormone, excitatory peptide, FMRFa, MIP or myomodulin signaling.
source: In Platynereis, autoregulation of cells in the ANS can occur through allatotropin/orexin, NPY4, achatin, diuretic hormone, excitatory peptide, FMRFa, MIP or myomodulin signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the co-expression analysis.

claim: Autoregulation occurs in cells where co-expression of the neuropeptide and its corresponding deorphanized receptor occurs in the same cell.
source: These are cells where co-expression of the neuropeptide and its corresponding deorphanized receptor occurs in the same cell, based on the single cell RNA-Seq data analysis.
evidence: This is stated as the basis for identifying autoregulation.

claim: A high diversity of neuropeptide receptor expression has been reported for the mouse hypothalamus.
source: A high diversity of neuropeptide receptor expression has also been reported for the mouse hypothalamus (Campbell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior research.

claim: There is more extensive peptidergic integration within neurosecretory centers than was previously appreciated.
source: These observations suggest that there is more extensive peptidergic integration within these centers than was previously appreciated.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the findings.

claim: Neurosecretory centers may function as chemical brains wired by neuropeptide signaling where the specificity is derived not from direct synaptic connections but by peptide-receptor matching.
source: Neurosecretory centers may thus also function as chemical brains wired by neuropeptide signaling where the specificity is derived not from direct synaptic connections but by peptide-receptor matching.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Given a high enough number of specific peptide-receptor pairs and allowing the possibility of combinatorial signaling, it is theoretically possible to wire arbitrarily complex neural networks.
source: Given a high enough number of specific peptide-receptor pairs and allowing the possibility of combinatorial signaling, it is theoretically possible to wire arbitrarily complex neural networks.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical speculation.

claim: Complex signaling is already occurring between the cells of the ANS before any endocrine signals are released to the other regions of the body.
source: We interpret these results as an indication that complex signaling is already occurring between the cells of the ANS before any endocrine signals are released to the other regions of the body.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The Platynereis larval ANS expressed the neuropeptides FMRFa and vasotocin, suggesting this region has homology to the vertebrate hypothalamus.
source: Previously, it was found that the Platynereis larval ANS expressed the neuropeptides FMRFa and vasotocin, suggesting this region has homology to the vertebrate hypothalamus (Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Tessmar-Raible, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: Orthologs of additional neuropeptides known to be involved in hypothalamic signaling, including NPY, orexin, tachykinin, galanin and somatostatin, were assigned to the Platynereis ANS.
source: Through the analyses carried out here, we could assign orthologs of additional neuropeptides known to be involved in hypothalamic signaling, including NPY, orexin, tachykinin, galanin and somatostatin, to the Platynereis ANS.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Shared molecular fingerprints relating to circadian rhythmicity were identified between the Platynereis ANS and mouse hypothalamus.
source: By comparing the Platynereis ANS scRNA-seq data to scRNA-seq data from mouse hypothalamus, we could also identify shared molecular fingerprints relating to circadian rhythmicity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: These molecular similarities strengthen the argument for an evolutionary relationship between the ANS and the hypothalamus.
source: These molecular similarities strengthen the argument for an evolutionary relationship between the ANS and the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the molecular similarities.

claim: The Platynereis ANS incorporates the ciliary photoreceptor cells, previously postulated to function in non-visual light detection for regulating circadian cycles in the free-swimming larvae.
source: The Platynereis ANS incorporates the ciliary photoreceptor cells, previously postulated to function in non-visual light detection for regulating circadian cycles in the free-swimming larvae (Tosches et al. 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior research.

claim: The ANS includes a subset of cells associated with the Platynereis larval apical sensory organ, namely the central-most cells such as SNWLD, SNIRP2, and SNMIP, implicated to play a role in larval settlement.
source: The ANS also includes a subset of cells associated with the Platynereis larval apical sensory organ (Marlow et al., 2014). These are namely the central-most cells of the ANS, such as SNWLD, SNIRP2, and SNMIP, implicated to play a role in larval settlement (Marlow et al., 2014; Conzelmann et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: Not all cells of the apical organ project to the ANS neuropil; the mechanosensory cells bypass this neurosecretory center to synapse on a separate synaptic circuit.
source: Not all cells of the apical organ as described by Marlow et al. project to the ANS neuropil, however – the mechanosensory cells bypass this neurosecretory center to synapse on a separate synaptic circuit (unpublished results).
evidence: This is stated as an unpublished observation.

claim: In many marine invertebrate larvae, the apical sensory organ is lost following settlement and metamorphosis.
source: In many marine invertebrate larvae, the apical sensory organ is lost following settlement and metamorphosis (Nielsen 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior research.

claim: While the central ciliated crescent cell is lost in 6-day-old settled postlarvae, the sensory cells SNWLD, SNMIP, and SNIRP2 remain and may continue to play a sensory-neurosecretory role later in the life cycle.
source: We found that while the central ciliated crescent cell is lost in 6-day-old settled postlarvae, the sensory cells SNWLD, SNMIP, and SNIRP2 remain and may continue to play a sensory-neurosecretory role later in the life cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Parts of the larval nervous system are thought to persist in the adult nervous system in Platynereis.
source: In Platynereis, parts of the larval nervous system are thought to persist in the adult nervous system, however exactly which cells remain into adulthood beyond the 6-day-old postlarval stage has not yet been described at the level of specific individual cells.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a caveat about what is not yet known.

claim: The sensory systems of the ciliary photoreceptors and nuchal organs, which project to the ANS neuropil, remain into adulthood.
source: Certainly the sensory systems of the ciliary photoreceptors and nuchal organs, which project to the ANS neuropil, remain into adulthood (Orrhage and Müller, 2005; Purschke, 2005; Zantke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: The ANS initially integrates environmental cues for regulating larval swimming and settlement behavior in free-swimming, non-feeding Platynereis larvae, and will later integrate environmental cues to regulate the timing of feeding and other cyclic behavioral or physiological activities.
source: This suggests that the ANS, which initially integrates environmental cues for regulating larval swimming and settlement behavior in free-swimming, non-feeding Platynereis larvae, will later integrate environmental cues in order to regulate the timing of feeding and other cyclic behavioral or physiological activities, likely including the maintenance of circadian rhythm throughout the life cycle (Zantke et al. 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with a citation.

claim: The neuropeptides investigated continue to be expressed during the adult stages of the Platynereis life cycle.
source: The neuropeptides investigated here also continue to be expressed during the adult stages of the Platynereis life cycle (Conzelmann et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior research.

claim: Neuropeptide function in Platynereis adult stages has not yet been characterized.
source: Neuropeptide function in Platynereis adult stages has not yet been characterized
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: In other annelid groups - leeches and earthworms - vasopressin/oxytocin family peptide hormones induce adult reproductive behavior or egg-laying behavior respectively.
source: however, in other annelid groups - leeches and earthworms - vasopressin/oxytocin family peptide hormones induce adult reproductive behavior or egg-laying behavior respectively (Oumi et al., 1996; Wagenaar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: The ANS, a primarily neurosecretory anterior brain region, is directly sensory in Platynereis, possibly reflecting an ancestral condition for neurosecretory centers.
source: The ANS, a primarily neurosecretory anterior brain region, is directly sensory in Platynereis, possibly reflecting an ancestral condition for neurosecretory centers (Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Hartenstein, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a speculative interpretation and citations.

claim: An anatomically and molecularly distinct 'chemical' and 'synaptic' brain as found in the Platynereis larva may have originated early in the evolution of the nervous system.
source: An anatomically and molecularly distinct 'chemical' and 'synaptic' brain as we found in the Platynereis larva may have originated early in the evolution of the nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation.

claim: This idea is consistent with the chimeric brain hypothesis, which posits the fusion of a neurosecretory and a synaptic nervous system early in animal evolution.
source: This idea is consistent with the chimeric brain hypothesis, which posits the fusion of a neurosecretory and a synaptic nervous system early in animal evolution (Tosches and Arendt, 2013) and is also supported by the distinct molecular signature of ANS cells (Achim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: The projection interneurons and ciliary photoreceptor cells exhibit features of both the chemical (dense core vesicles, neuropeptide and GPCR expression) and synaptic (large synapses with clear vesicles, neurotransmitter marker expression) nervous system cell types.
source: Interestingly, the projection interneurons and ciliary photoreceptor cells exhibit features of both the chemical (dense core vesicles, neuropeptide and GPCR expression) and synaptic (large synapses with clear vesicles, neurotransmitter marker expression) nervous system cell types.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: The dual peptidergic-synaptic nature of the projection interneurons enables them to act as translators of environmental cues integrated through the ANS into locomotor outputs in the synaptic nervous system.
source: The dual peptidergic-synaptic nature of the projection interneurons, which are themselves under peptidergic control, enables them to act as translators of environmental cues integrated through the ANS into locomotor outputs in the synaptic nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the dual nature of these neurons.

claim: The INRGW projection interneurons link the sensory-neurosecretory ANS to the serotonergic ciliomotor neurons through synaptic connections.
source: Specifically, the INRGW projection interneurons link the sensory-neurosecretory ANS to the serotonergic ciliomotor neurons through synaptic connections.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: This would allow regulation of ciliary swimming, a larva-specific feature.
source: This would allow regulation of ciliary swimming, a larva-specific feature.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the connectivity.

claim: Neuropeptides are ideal molecules for chemical signaling due to their small size and high diversity.
source: Neuropeptides are ideal molecules for chemical signaling due to their small size and high diversity.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge.

claim: Many of the neuropeptides expressed in the Platynereis ANS and the vertebrate hypothalamus belong to ancient peptide families that evolved close to the origin of the nervous system.
source: Many of the neuropeptides expressed in the Platynereis ANS and the vertebrate hypothalamus belong to ancient peptide families that evolved close to the origin of the nervous system (Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: Neuropeptide genes have been identified in bilaterians, cnidarians, and even the early-branching metazoan Trichoplax adhaerens, that lacks a synaptic nervous system but has neurosecretory cells.
source: Neuropeptide genes have been identified in bilaterians, cnidarians, and even the early-branching metazoan Trichoplax adhaerens, that lacks a synaptic nervous system but has neurosecretory cells (Nikitin, 2015; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior research.

claim: Chemical signaling by neuropeptides may have been important early during nervous system evolution in small metazoans where only peptide diffusion could coordinate physiological activities and behavior.
source: Chemical signaling by neuropeptides may have been important early during nervous system evolution in small metazoans where only peptide diffusion could coordinate physiological activities and behavior (Varoqueaux and Fasshauer, 2017; Senatore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation with citations.

claim: As metazoans grew larger, the coordination of their large complex bodies required control by a synaptic nervous system.
source: As metazoans grew larger, the coordination of their large complex bodies required control by a synaptic nervous system (Keijzer and Arnellos, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior research.

claim: The separate origins of the chemical and the synaptic nervous system may still be reflected to varying degrees in contemporary brains.
source: The separate origins of the chemical and the synaptic nervous system may still be reflected to varying degrees in contemporary brains.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation.

claim: The Platynereis larval nervous system, and possibly the nervous system of other marine invertebrate larvae, shows a particularly clear segregation of non-synaptic and synaptic nervous systems.
source: The Platynereis larval nervous system, and possibly the nervous system of other marine invertebrate larvae, shows a particularly clear segregation of non-synaptic and synaptic nervous systems.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a speculative extension to other larvae.

claim: The extent of non-synaptic signaling, even in the relatively simple nervous system of the Platynereis larva, highlights the importance of the combined study of connectomes and chemical signaling networks.
source: The extent of non-synaptic signaling, even in the relatively simple nervous system of the Platynereis larva, highlights the importance of the combined study of connectomes and chemical signaling networks.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The ssTEM dataset consists of 4845 layers of 40 nm thin sections.
source: The dataset consists of 4845 layers of 40 nm thin sections.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The cells were reconstructed, reviewed, 3D visualized, and the resulting synaptic network was analyzed in Catmaid.
source: The cells were reconstructed, reviewed, 3D visualized, and the resulting synaptic network was analyzed in Catmaid (Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section with citations for the software.
